name: Jade Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and answer warranty calls and chats about washing machines at a contact centre. I finished secondary school and know the claim rules well enough to spot a wrong model number, though I am an ordinary experienced agent, not a supervisor. Weekend cover brings my pay above the usual agent rate. Every day I use the approved AI claim summary, then check the original receipt, serial label and warranty terms before promising a repair.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What matters outside work when you think about changing jobs?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Theo works at a garden supply counter, and our children have grown up and moved out. We rent, have about nine months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other contact centres nearby. I would miss the weekend rate if I moved, but I would also like one whole Saturday with Theo now and again. We have no confirmed income to replace my wage when I eventually stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team that the claim summary is handy, but a serial number still decides whether a repair is covered. Last Tuesday a customer read out one digit wrong and the screen confidently described another machine. I caught it by opening her receipt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I can keep earning the weekend rate if the warranty queue stays about this size. Our nine-month reserve is real, though it is the roof-repair money as much as the job-search money. I would rather keep that buffer than gamble it on a fashionable course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my warranty shifts and check receipts against the approved AI summary as I do now. Each month while the weekend premium is paid, I would put forty from it into the roof fund. I would write down what a full week at a nearby centre actually pays, but I am not applying over a small shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly settled. It would be pleasant to end a chat faster without telling a customer the wrong repair date. The roof still nags at me more than the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep checking the original paperwork if the summary seemed reliable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the original receipt beside the AI summary, even if the summary saves two minutes. A repaired machine is no good to a customer if I have promised the wrong part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the roof fund. Would the extra saving continue if your weekend rate changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo and I have already talked about the roof, so the forty is a modest monthly addition while the weekend rate lasts. If the premium disappears, I would stop that addition before promising to spend the existing reserve.

I would show them the **wrong-model case** that I caught on the customer’s receipt.
think: I think the **weekend rate** can last if the warranty queue stays near its present size.
I regard our **nine-month reserve** as roof money as well as job-search money.
do: Keep **warranty shifts** and compare approved AI summaries with original receipts.
Add **forty monthly** to the roof fund only while the weekend premium continues.
Record **full-week pay** at nearby centres without applying over a minor shortcut.
feel: I feel **settled** about work, with the roof expense still on my mind.

fieldNote: The **serial label** anchors her confidence in checking AI output.

She notes nearby pay but makes **no application** in this picture.

steps.text: Keep warranty shifts and check AI summaries against original receipts

Record full-week pay at nearby centres without applying over minor shortcuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that a bot can answer a standard warranty question before I finish saying hello. Customers with a leak under the machine will still want someone to own the repair booking. I would ask our manager to put the new rota and paid checking time in writing, because a cheerful briefing is not a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think fewer routine chats could mean fewer weekend hours for me. Theo’s counter wage covers part of our rent, but my higher rate pays a lot of the bills. Nine months saved gives me room to test a change; it does not make missing pay harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: During paid time, if the claims log permits it, I would learn the new AI claim checker on twenty closed cases and note where it mistakes a serial number or warranty date. I would keep taking live claims and ask the manager for written weekend hours before changing our household budget. If paid weekend hours actually fall, I would start comparing posted repair-booking counter jobs with full weekly wage and hours after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, edging toward anxious when I picture a shorter rota. I like learning a tool, but liking a tool will not pay our utility bill. I can search nearby, which keeps this from feeling like a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test the checker on live claims?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not run live customers through an unapproved checker. I would use the twenty closed files only during paid time and only if their use is permitted; otherwise I would wait for an approved test set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would make you start looking for another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first look at the written weekend rota, not a headline hourly rate. If it shrinks, I would compare the complete weekly pay and hours at posted counter jobs after travel before applying; I would keep my current paid shifts until a suitable offer is signed.

say: I would say **standard claims** may move to a bot while urgent repair bookings still need an owner.
I would ask for the **written rota** and paid checking time before trusting a briefing.
think: I fear **weekend hours** could shrink as routine chats move to AI.
I know Theo’s wage helps rent, but my **higher rate** pays many bills.
do: Learn the **new AI checker** on twenty permitted closed cases during paid time; otherwise wait for an approved test set.
Keep **live warranty claims** and seek written weekend hours before changing the household budget.
If weekend hours fall, compare **posted counter jobs** by complete weekly wage/hours after travel; apply only if suitable, leave when signed.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about a shorter rota but able to search nearby.
S1.quote: I would ask our manager to put the new rota and paid checking time in writing, because a cheerful briefing is not a shift.
fieldNote: She distinguishes an **approved test** from trying AI on live customers.
A written **weekly rota** matters more to her than a posted hourly rate.
She has a **search option**, though the lost premium would affect bills.

steps.text: Learn new AI checker on twenty permitted closed cases during paid time
Keep live warranty claims while seeking written weekend hours
Compare posted counter jobs after weekend cuts by full weekly pay and hours after travel
Apply only if suitable after cuts; leave paid shifts when offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the warranty chat queue could empty before we have even changed the rota. A machine can read the receipt and policy together faster than my team can. I would want the company to tell us actual paid shift dates rather than invite us to admire a demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my weekend premium could vanish by 2028, and the nine-month reserve would then become a clock. Theo’s garden-counter pay cannot carry rent and utilities alone. Many centres sit on the bus route, but I would need their real weekly hours, not an attractive hourly rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now in 2026 I would put the last eight weekly payslips beside our rent, utilities and bus fare. If my paid shifts end after 2028, I would apply for posted paid service-counter work only where the written weekly wage and hours cover those costs after travel. I would stay on paid warranty shifts until a suitable signed offer arrives, and I would not spend more than six weeks of our reserve searching before reviewing the plan with Theo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about an abrupt end to the premium. I have enough saved to look, and I can learn a different counter’s rules. I would still hate explaining to Theo that a pretty job advert was only two shifts a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use all nine months of savings in that search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, six weeks is a review point for using existing savings, not a promise to stop looking or an amount I can afford to lose. Theo and I would recalculate the bills and any actual offers then. We would not treat the whole nine months as spare cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to know about a service-counter job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the new desk can approve a replacement appliance or only send a message to someone else. I would weigh the answer before accepting, because a desk that cannot resolve a claim may lose its queue too. The hard figures are still the posted paid opening, the written full-week wage and hours, and the fare home.

say: I would warn colleagues that **warranty chats** could disappear before a new rota is agreed.
I would ask for **actual paid dates**, not a demonstration of the software.
think: I fear my **weekend premium** could vanish by 2028.
I know Theo’s wage cannot cover **rent and utilities** without mine.
do: Set **eight weekly payslips** beside rent, utilities and bus fares in 2026.
If paid shifts end after 2028, apply for **posted paid counters** with written weekly wage/hours covering rent/utilities after fare; leave when signed.
Review use of **existing reserve** with Theo after at most six weeks of searching.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing paid shifts quickly, while nine months saved permits a search.
S2.quote: Many centres sit on the bus route, but I would need their real weekly hours, not an attractive hourly rate.
fieldNote: The **six-week review** limits use of existing savings; it is not new saving.
She asks about **claim authority** but does not make it a hard job condition.
The job move needs a **posted paid opening**, written full-week terms and a signed offer.

steps.text: Compare eight weekly payslips with rent, utilities and bus fares in 2026
Apply if paid shifts end after 2028: posted paid counter, written rent/utility-covering weekly pay/hours after fare
Keep paid warranty shifts until a suitable service-counter offer is signed
Review reserve use with Theo after at most six search weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team we have time to show exactly which warranty errors cost customers another week without a washer. Robots in showrooms may come around 2034, but the claim decisions on my screen could change in 2031. I would ask for paid time to check the new claim system against real closed cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years lets me build a record of the errors I catch, but it does not guarantee my weekend hours. My strength is explaining a repair delay and getting a technician booked, not typing a rule faster than a machine. I would prefer a paid service desk where I can actually authorise the next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep a permitted log of twenty corrected claims while doing paid warranty work. If our paid hours fall as 2031 arrives, I would apply to posted paid appliance-service counters with authority to approve a booking, written weekly wage and hours covering rent and utilities after travel. I would keep my current shifts until that offer is signed; if no such opening exists, I would keep checking nearby centres rather than pay for an unrequired certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my paid hours shrinking as 2031 approaches, although five years gives me room to show my work. I cannot tell which employer will still pay the weekend rate. The permitted corrections log gives me something practical to show, but no guarantee of a full rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in the log, and when would you make it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The log would use only claims the centre permits us to study, with customer details removed, and I would make it on paid time. I would show a manager the corrected booking dates, not just claim I am good with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any service-desk title be enough to make you switch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the service desk to show me who can authorise a repair visit. If I can only forward messages, I would not switch for the same weekly pay. I would also check the written weekly hours and the travel bill before agreeing to leave my paid calls.

say: I would show the team **corrected claim errors** that delayed real repairs.
I would ask for **paid checking time** before the 2031 screen change.
think: I think a **five-year record** may help, but it cannot secure weekend hours.
I value **booking authority** more than a new service-desk title.
do: Keep **twenty corrected claims** in a permitted, de-identified log during paid warranty time.
If paid hours fall around 2031, apply for **posted paid service desks** with booking authority and written rent/utility-covering weekly wage/hours after travel.
Keep **paid calls** until a suitable signed offer; otherwise keep checking nearby centres without buying an unrequired certificate.
feel: I feel **anxious** because my paid weekend hours may shrink as 2031 approaches.
I have **time to prepare**, but the corrections log cannot guarantee a full rota.
S3.quote: My strength is explaining a repair delay and getting a technician booked, not typing a rule faster than a machine.
fieldNote: She wants a **permitted log** of errors, not a public claim database.
A counter needs real **booking authority** as well as sufficient full-week pay.
She rejects an **unrequired certificate** as a speculative purchase.

steps.text: Log twenty permitted de-identified corrections during paid warranty work
Apply after 2031 cuts: posted paid desk, booking authority, written rent/utility-covering weekly pay/hours after travel
Keep paid calls until a suitable service-desk offer is signed
Check nearby centres if no suitable service-desk opening exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Theo that a decade lets us compare several years of real household pay, not guess at a retirement date. Thinking AI could take claim decisions by 2036; robots visiting kitchens would be a later question around 2039. I would still ask the centre what paid weekend work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years gives me time to work out whether we can afford fewer Saturdays or whether I still need the premium. I cannot count on a retirement payment that we have not verified. Nine months saved feels comfortable until a roof bill and a long gap in wages arrive together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each year from now I would put our actual wages, rent, utilities and roof costs on one page and check any retirement income only when it is confirmed. I would keep paid warranty work while it covers our bills. If weekend hours fall after 2036 and we still need my wage, I would compare posted paid service-desk openings by written weekly wage and hours after travel, and leave only on a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly calm about the longer runway, though I do not think the calendar does the arithmetic for us. I would like a free Saturday with Theo, but not at the cost of using the roof fund to pay ordinary rent. A slow plan feels possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would 2036 make you set a retirement date now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not choose a date just because the card says 2036. We would need verified income and a year-by-year picture of rent and bills before deciding whether I could reduce work. I am comfortable saying we do not know yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you still need your wage when the weekend rota shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I still need the wage and weekend hours shrink, I would look at paid service counters before I give notice. I would check the complete written week, the bus fare and the signature, as I said in the faster pictures. The roof fund is for the roof unless our bills force a new decision.

think: I need **verified income** before choosing whether to work fewer Saturdays.
I know the **roof bill** and a wage gap could use our reserve together.
do: Compare **actual wages**, rent, utilities, roof costs and any verified retirement income each year.
Keep **paid warranty work** while its full weekly wage covers household bills.
After 2036 cuts, if wages remain needed, compare **posted paid desks** by written weekly pay/hours covering rent/utilities after travel; leave when signed.
feel: I feel **mostly calm** about time to plan, with the cost of a roof bill still in mind.
S4.quote: Nine months saved feels comfortable until a roof bill and a long gap in wages arrive together.
fieldNote: A decade enables **yearly comparisons**, not an assumed retirement date.
She keeps the **roof fund** for repairs unless bills force a new decision.
Any move remains gated by **paid hours**, household costs and a signed offer.

steps.text: Compare actual wages, rent, utilities, roof costs and verified retirement income yearly
Keep paid warranty work while full-week wage covers household bills
Compare posted paid service desks if post-2036 hours fall and wages remain needed
Leave only for signed written weekly wage/hours covering bills after travel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our weekend paid hours could vanish before I have checked another full-week offer. Nine months saved and nearby centres let me search, but neither replaces the premium automatically. Written shift dates at my current centre and posted paid counter jobs with clear weekly wage and hours would help me make a decision with Theo.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens when a customer has no machine for a week because a claim summary got a model wrong. Someone has to own correcting the wrong appliance model, whether the company calls it AI work or service work.

headlineQuote: Someone has to own correcting the wrong appliance model, whether the company calls it AI work or service work.
portrait: At **58**, Jade is an experienced warranty agent with secondary school education, a higher weekend rate and daily approved AI use.
She and Theo have **nine months saved**, grown children elsewhere and many nearby centres, but no verified retirement income.
She tests the **new claim checker** on permitted closed cases during paid time as routine chats shrink.
She needs **written full-week pay** covering rent and bills after travel, plus a signed offer, before changing jobs.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could end paid weekend hours before a suitable new offer appears.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written shift dates** and posted paid counter openings with clear weekly wage and hours.
